papers.title: Areas: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on areas, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A rhombus has diagonals of length 10 cm and 16 cm. Find its area.
questions.explanation:
Area of a rhombus $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times d_{1} \times d_{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 16 = 80$ cm²

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $26$ cm²: You added the diagonals. Area of a rhombus $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times d_{1} \times d_{2}$.
- $40$ cm²: You took a quarter of the product. The diagonals split the rhombus into four triangles of area $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 8$ each.
- $160$ cm²: You forgot the $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: The circumference of a circular mat is 44 cm. Find its area. [Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$]
questions.explanation:
$2\pi r = 44 \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{44 \times 7}{2 \times 22} = 7$ cm.

Area $= \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ cm²

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $77$ cm²: You halved the area. $A = \pi r^{2}$ with $r = 7$.
- $308$ cm²: You used $2\pi r^{2}$. The area of a circle is $\pi r^{2}$.
- $49$ cm²: You worked out $r^{2} = 49$ and forgot to multiply by $\pi$.

questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 10 cm has an arc length of 15 cm. Find the area of the sector.
questions.explanation:
Area of a sector $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times r \times l = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 15 = 75$ cm².

(This comes from $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^{2}$ with $\dfrac{\theta}{360} = \dfrac{l}{2\pi r}$.)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $7.5$ cm²: You halved the arc length. Area of a sector $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times r \times \text{arc length}$.
- $150$ cm²: You forgot the $\dfrac{1}{2}$: area $= \dfrac{1}{2}rl$.
- $100\pi$ cm²: $100\pi$ is the area of the whole circle, not the sector.

questions.stem: Find the area of an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm, leaving your answer in surd form.
questions.explanation:
Area $= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 6 \times \sin 60° = 18 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 9\sqrt{3}$ cm²

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $18$ cm²: You used $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 6$. The height is not 6 cm; use $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin 60°$.
- $18\sqrt{3}$ cm²: You forgot the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$.
- $36$ cm²: 36 cm² is the area of a 6 cm square.

questions.stem: A circular flower bed of radius 3.5 m has a path around it, so that the outer edge of the path is a circle of radius 7 m. Find the area of the path. [Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$]
questions.explanation:
Area of path $= \pi R^{2} - \pi r^{2} = \dfrac{22}{7}(49 - 12.25) = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 36.75 = 115.5$ m²

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $462$ m²: You used the diameters, 14 m and 7 m, as the radii.
- $154$ m²: 154 m² is the area of the outer circle. Subtract the flower bed.
- $192.5$ m²: You added the two areas.

papers.title: Lengths and Perimeters: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on lengths and perimeters, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An arc of length 22 cm is on a circle of radius 14 cm. Find the angle the arc subtends at the centre. [Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$]
questions.explanation:
Circumference $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = 88$ cm.

$\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 88 = 22 \Rightarrow \theta = \dfrac{22 \times 360}{88} = 90°$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $45°$: You used the diameter, 28 cm, as the radius.
- $180°$: You used $\pi r$ instead of $2\pi r$ for the circumference.
- $270°$: 270° is the angle of the major arc. The 22 cm arc is a quarter of the circle.

questions.stem: Find the perimeter of a semicircular plot of land with a diameter of 28 m. [Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$]
questions.explanation:
Curved edge $= \dfrac{1}{2}\pi d = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 44$ m.

Perimeter $= 44 + 28 = 72$ m

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $44$ m: 44 m is the curved edge only. Add the straight edge (the diameter).
- $88$ m: 88 m is the circumference of the whole circle.
- $116$ m: You added the diameter to the whole circumference. A semicircle has half the circumference.

questions.stem: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 70 cm. How many complete turns does it make in travelling 1.1 km? [Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$]
questions.explanation:
One turn $= \pi d = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 70 = 220$ cm. 1.1 km $= 110\,000$ cm.

Turns $= \dfrac{110\,000}{220} = 500$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $5$: You did not convert 1.1 km to centimetres: 1.1 km = 110 000 cm.
- $250$: You used the diameter as the radius: $2\pi \times 70 = 440$ cm.
- $1000$: You used $\pi r$ for the circumference. One turn covers $\pi d = 220$ cm.

questions.stem: A rectangle has an area of 48 cm² and a width of 6 cm. Find its perimeter.
questions.explanation:
Length $= 48 \div 6 = 8$ cm.

Perimeter $= 2(8 + 6) = 28$ cm

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $14$ cm: 14 cm is the length plus the width. The perimeter goes all the way round: $2(l + w)$.
- $54$ cm: You added the area and the width.
- $96$ cm: You doubled the area.

questions.stem: The area of a circle is 616 cm². Find its circumference. [Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$]
questions.explanation:
$\pi r^{2} = 616 \Rightarrow r^{2} = 616 \times \dfrac{7}{22} = 196 \Rightarrow r = 14$ cm.

Circumference $= 2\pi r = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = 88$ cm

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $44$ cm: You used $\pi r$. The circumference is $2\pi r$.
- $176$ cm: You used the diameter, 28 cm, as the radius.
- $14$ cm: 14 cm is the radius. The question asks for the circumference, $2\pi r$.

papers.title: Polygons: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on polygons, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 24°. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation:
The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°.

Number of sides $= \dfrac{360°}{24°} = 15$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $7.5$: You divided 180° by 24°. The exterior angles add up to 360°.
- $24$: 24 is the size of each exterior angle, not the number of sides.
- $156$: 156° is the interior angle, $180° - 24°$, not the number of sides.

questions.stem: Find the sum of the exterior angles of a nonagon (a polygon with 9 sides).
questions.explanation:
The exterior angles of any convex polygon, whatever the number of sides, add up to 360°.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $40°$: 40° is each exterior angle of a regular nonagon. The question asks for the sum.
- $140°$: 140° is each interior angle of a regular nonagon.
- $1260°$: 1260° is the sum of the interior angles, $(9 - 2) \times 180°$.

questions.stem: Find the size of each interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides).
questions.explanation:
Sum of interior angles $= (10 - 2) \times 180° = 1440°$; each angle $= 1440° \div 10 = 144°$.

(Or: exterior angle $= 360° \div 10 = 36°$; interior $= 180° - 36° = 144°$.)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $36°$: 36° is each exterior angle. The interior angle is $180° - 36°$.
- $1440°$: 1440° is the sum of the interior angles. Divide by 10.
- $1800°$: You used $n \times 180°$. The angle sum is $(n - 2) \times 180°$.

questions.stem: The interior angles of a hexagon are $2x°$, $3x°$, 110°, 120°, 130° and 140°. Find $x$.
questions.explanation:
Sum of interior angles of a hexagon $= (6 - 2) \times 180° = 720°$.

$2x + 3x + 110 + 120 + 130 + 140 = 720 \Rightarrow 5x = 220 \Rightarrow x = 44$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $8$: You used 540°, the angle sum of a pentagon. A hexagon's angles add up to 720°.
- $116$: You used 1080°, the angle sum of an octagon.
- $220$: $5x = 220$, so you must still divide by 5.

questions.stem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is four times each exterior angle. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.explanation:
Interior + exterior $= 180°$: $4e + e = 180° \Rightarrow e = 36°$.

Number of sides $= 360° \div 36° = 10$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $4$: 4 is the ratio of the angles, not the number of sides.
- $36$: 36° is the exterior angle. Divide 360° by it.
- $144$: 144° is the interior angle, not the number of sides.

papers.title: Matrices and Determinants: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on matrices and determinants, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Given that $A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, find $A - 2B$.
questions.explanation:
$2B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 8 \\ 6 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$

$A - 2B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 - 4 & 2 - 8 \\ 1 - 6 & 3 - 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -6 \\ -5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$: That is $A - B$. Multiply every entry of $B$ by 2 first.
- $\begin{pmatrix} 9 & 10 \\ 7 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$: You added $2B$ instead of subtracting it.
- $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$: Watch the signs: $2 - 8 = -6$ and $1 - 6 = -5$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.
questions.explanation:
Row 1: $2 \times 3 + (-1) \times 2 = 4$. Row 2: $3 \times 3 + 4 \times 2 = 17$.

Result: $\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 17 \end{pmatrix}$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $\begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 17 \end{pmatrix}$: In the top row, $2 \times 3 + (-1) \times 2 = 6 - 2 = 4$: the sign of $-1$ was dropped.
- $\begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$: You multiplied the columns of the matrix by the vector. Use each row: row × column.
- $\begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 17 \end{pmatrix}$: Check the top entry: $6 - 2 = +4$.

questions.stem: For what value of $k$ is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} k & 4 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ singular?
questions.explanation:
A matrix is singular when its determinant is 0.

$6k - 4 \times 3 = 0 \Rightarrow 6k = 12 \Rightarrow k = 2$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $-2$: The determinant is $6k - 12$, not $6k + 12$.
- $4.5$: You multiplied the wrong pairs: the determinant is $k \times 6 - 4 \times 3$.
- $0$: A singular matrix has determinant 0; that does not make $k = 0$. With $k = 0$ the determinant is $-12$.

questions.stem: Given that $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 7 \\ 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$ and $2X + A = B$, find the matrix $X$.
questions.explanation:
$2X = B - A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$, so $X = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 4 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}$: That is $2X$. Divide every entry by 2.
- $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix}$: You added $A$ instead of subtracting it: $2X = B - A$.
- $\begin{pmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 \end{pmatrix}$: You worked out $A - B$. Move $A$ to the other side: $2X = B - A$.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix with determinant 5. Find the determinant of $2A$.
questions.explanation:
If $A = \begin{pmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{pmatrix}$ then $2A = \begin{pmatrix} 2p & 2q \\ 2r & 2s \end{pmatrix}$, and

$\det(2A) = 2p \times 2s - 2q \times 2r = 4(ps - qr) = 4 \times 5 = 20$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $7$: You added 2 to the determinant.
- $10$: Multiplying a $2 \times 2$ matrix by 2 doubles every entry, so the determinant is multiplied by $2 \times 2 = 4$.
- $25$: 25 is $5^{2}$. The determinant of $2A$ is $2^{2} \times 5$.

papers.title: Transformations: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on transformations, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Find the image of the point $(-4, 3)$ after a reflection in the $y$-axis.
questions.explanation:
A reflection in the $y$-axis changes the sign of the $x$-coordinate: $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$.

$(-4, 3) \to (4, 3)$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $(-4, -3)$: That is a reflection in the $x$-axis, which changes the sign of $y$.
- $(4, -3)$: That is a half-turn about the origin: both signs change.
- $(3, -4)$: That is a reflection in the line $y = x$: the coordinates swap.

questions.stem: The point $(2, -5)$ is rotated through 180° about the origin. Find its image.
questions.explanation:
A rotation of 180° about the origin changes both signs: $(x, y) \to (-x, -y)$.

$(2, -5) \to (-2, 5)$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $(5, 2)$: That is a rotation of 90° anticlockwise: $(x, y) \to (-y, x)$.
- $(-5, -2)$: That is a rotation of 90° clockwise: $(x, y) \to (y, -x)$.
- $(2, 5)$: That is a reflection in the $x$-axis.

questions.stem: Find the image of the point $(3, 1)$ after a reflection in the line $y = -x$.
questions.explanation:
A reflection in $y = -x$ maps $(x, y) \to (-y, -x)$.

$(3, 1) \to (-1, -3)$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $(1, 3)$: That is a reflection in $y = x$. In $y = -x$ the coordinates swap and both change sign.
- $(-3, -1)$: That is a half-turn about the origin: the coordinates do not swap.
- $(3, -1)$: That is a reflection in the $x$-axis.

questions.stem: The point $(3, -1)$ is enlarged with centre the origin and scale factor $-2$. Find its image.
questions.explanation:
With centre the origin, multiply each coordinate by the scale factor:

$(3 \times (-2),\ -1 \times (-2)) = (-6, 2)$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $(-1.5, 0.5)$: You divided by $-2$. An enlargement multiplies the coordinates by the scale factor.
- $(-6, -2)$: Multiply both coordinates by $-2$: $-1 \times (-2) = +2$.
- $(6, -2)$: You ignored the negative sign. A negative scale factor puts the image on the other side of the centre.

questions.stem: A translation maps the point $(1, 4)$ onto $(-2, 6)$. Find the image of the point $(5, -3)$ under the same translation.
questions.explanation:
Translation vector $= \begin{pmatrix} -2 - 1 \\ 6 - 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

Image of $(5, -3) = (5 - 3,\ -3 + 2) = (2, -1)$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $(-3, 2)$: $(-3, 2)$ is the translation vector, not the image.
- $(2, 1)$: Check the second coordinate: $-3 + 2 = -1$.
- $(8, -5)$: You subtracted the translation vector instead of adding it.

papers.title: Cumulative Frequency: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on cumulative frequency, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem:
The table shows the heights of 40 seedlings in a school nursery.

$$
\begin{array}{l|ccccc}
\text{Height (cm)} & \text{1–5} & \text{6–10} & \text{11–15} & \text{16–20} & \text{21–25} \\ \hline
\text{Frequency} & 3 & 7 & 12 & 10 & 8
\end{array}
$$

What is the cumulative frequency of the class 11–15?
questions.explanation:
Running total up to 11–15: $3 + 7 + 12 = 22$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $10$: 10 is the cumulative frequency up to 6–10. Add the 12 seedlings in 11–15.
- $12$: 12 is the frequency of 11–15 alone. Cumulative frequency is the running total.
- $32$: 32 is the cumulative frequency up to 16–20, one class too far.

questions.stem:
The table shows the heights of 40 seedlings in a school nursery.

$$
\begin{array}{l|ccccc}
\text{Height (cm)} & \text{1–5} & \text{6–10} & \text{11–15} & \text{16–20} & \text{21–25} \\ \hline
\text{Frequency} & 3 & 7 & 12 & 10 & 8
\end{array}
$$

What is the upper class boundary of the class 11–15?
questions.explanation:
The upper class boundary lies halfway between the upper limit of this class (15) and the lower limit of the next (16): $15.5$.

Cumulative frequency curves are plotted against upper class boundaries.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $10.5$: 10.5 is the lower class boundary of 11–15.
- $15$: 15 is the upper class limit. The boundary is halfway between 15 and 16.
- $16$: 16 is the lower limit of the next class.

questions.stem:
The table shows the heights of 40 seedlings in a school nursery.

$$
\begin{array}{l|ccccc}
\text{Height (cm)} & \text{1–5} & \text{6–10} & \text{11–15} & \text{16–20} & \text{21–25} \\ \hline
\text{Frequency} & 3 & 7 & 12 & 10 & 8
\end{array}
$$

In which class does the median height lie?
questions.explanation:
There are 40 seedlings, so the median is the $\dfrac{40}{2} = 20$th value.

Cumulative frequencies: 3, 10, 22, 32, 40. The 20th value is past 10 but not past 22, so it is in 11–15.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 6–10: Only 10 seedlings are 10 cm or less, so the 20th is not in this class.
- 16–20: By 15 cm the running total is already 22, past the 20th seedling.
- 21–25: 21–25 is the last class; the middle of 40 values comes well before it.

questions.stem:
The table shows the heights of 40 seedlings in a school nursery.

$$
\begin{array}{l|ccccc}
\text{Height (cm)} & \text{1–5} & \text{6–10} & \text{11–15} & \text{16–20} & \text{21–25} \\ \hline
\text{Frequency} & 3 & 7 & 12 & 10 & 8
\end{array}
$$

How many seedlings are taller than 15.5 cm?
questions.explanation:
Taller than 15.5 cm means the classes 16–20 and 21–25: $10 + 8 = 18$. (Or $40 - 22 = 18$.)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $8$: You counted only the class 21–25. The class 16–20 is also taller than 15.5 cm.
- $22$: 22 seedlings are 15.5 cm or shorter. Subtract from 40.
- $10$: You counted only the class 16–20. The class 21–25 is also taller than 15.5 cm.

questions.stem:
The table shows the heights of 40 seedlings in a school nursery.

$$
\begin{array}{l|ccccc}
\text{Height (cm)} & \text{1–5} & \text{6–10} & \text{11–15} & \text{16–20} & \text{21–25} \\ \hline
\text{Frequency} & 3 & 7 & 12 & 10 & 8
\end{array}
$$

What percentage of the seedlings are 10 cm tall or less?
questions.explanation:
10 cm or less means 1–5 and 6–10: $3 + 7 = 10$ seedlings.

$\dfrac{10}{40} \times 100\% = 25\%$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 7.5%: You used only the class 1–5. Seedlings in 6–10 are also 10 cm or less.
- 17.5%: You used only the class 6–10. Add the 3 seedlings in 1–5.
- 55%: 55% is the percentage that are 15 cm or less.

papers.title: Statistics: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on statistics, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: On a pie chart showing the favourite fruits of 60 pupils, the sector for mango has an angle of 72°. How many pupils chose mango?
questions.explanation:
Number $= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 60 = \dfrac{1}{5} \times 60 = 12$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $1.2$: You divided 72 by 60. The fraction of the circle is $\dfrac{72}{360}$.
- $5$: You divided 360 by 72. Mango's share is $\dfrac{72}{360}$ of 60.
- $72$: 72 is the angle in degrees, not the number of pupils.

questions.stem: A family's monthly budget is Le 4,800, of which Le 1,800 is spent on food. What angle represents food on a pie chart of the budget?
questions.explanation:
Angle $= \dfrac{1800}{4800} \times 360° = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 360° = 135°$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $13.5°$: Check the decimal point: $\dfrac{1800}{4800} \times 360 = 135$.
- $37.5°$: 37.5 is the percentage spent on food, not the angle.
- $225°$: 225° is the angle for everything except food.

questions.stem: Which kind of chart is best for showing what fraction of a family's income is spent on each item?
questions.explanation:
A pie chart shows each part as a fraction of the whole: the angle of each sector is proportional to the amount.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- A line graph: A line graph shows how something changes over time.
- A histogram: A histogram shows the frequencies of grouped continuous data.
- A cumulative frequency curve: A cumulative frequency curve is used to find medians and quartiles.

questions.stem: What is the class width of the classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39?
questions.explanation:
Class width = upper boundary − lower boundary $= 19.5 - 9.5 = 10$. (Or the difference between the lower limits of two neighbouring classes, $20 - 10$.)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $9$: $19 - 10 = 9$ uses the class limits. The class boundaries are 9.5 and 19.5, so the width is 10.
- $19$: 19 is the upper limit of the first class.
- $20$: 20 is the lower limit of the second class.

questions.stem:
The table shows the number of children in 20 families.

$$
\begin{array}{l|cccc}
\text{Number of children} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline
\text{Number of families} & 4 & 6 & 7 & 3
\end{array}
$$

Find the mean number of children per family.
questions.explanation:
$\sum fx = 1(4) + 2(6) + 3(7) + 4(3) = 4 + 12 + 21 + 12 = 49$

Mean $= \dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f} = \dfrac{49}{20} = 2.45$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $2.5$: 2.5 is the mean of 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each value must be weighted by its frequency.
- $5$: 5 is the mean of the frequencies, $20 \div 4$.
- $12.25$: You divided $\sum fx = 49$ by 4. Divide by the number of families, 20.

papers.title: Measures of Dispersion: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on measures of dispersion, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Find the range of 4.5, 2.1, 7.8, 3.3 and 6.0.
questions.explanation:
Range $= \text{largest} - \text{smallest} = 7.8 - 2.1 = 5.7$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $3.3$: You subtracted the first number, 4.5, instead of the smallest, 2.1.
- $4.5$: You subtracted 3.3. The smallest number is 2.1.
- $9.9$: You added the largest and smallest. Range = largest − smallest.

questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of 4, 8 and 12, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation:
Mean $= 8$. Deviations: $-4, 0, 4$; squares: $16, 0, 16$.

Variance $= \dfrac{32}{3} = 10.67$; standard deviation $= \sqrt{10.67} = 3.27$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $8$: 8 is the range, $12 - 4$. The standard deviation measures spread about the mean.
- $5.66$: You did not divide $\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2} = 32$ by 3 before taking the square root.
- $10.67$: 10.67 is the variance. The standard deviation is its square root.

questions.stem: The standard deviation of a set of numbers is 3. Every number in the set is multiplied by 2. What is the new standard deviation?
questions.explanation:
Multiplying every value by 2 doubles every distance from the mean, so the standard deviation doubles: $2 \times 3 = 6$. (The variance is multiplied by 4.)

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $3$: Adding a number to every value leaves the standard deviation unchanged, but multiplying does not.
- $5$: You added 2. Multiplying every value by 2 doubles the spread.
- $12$: The variance is multiplied by $2^{2} = 4$, but the standard deviation only by 2.

questions.stem: From a cumulative frequency curve, the lower quartile of some marks is 24 and the upper quartile is 46. Find the semi-interquartile range.
questions.explanation:
Semi-interquartile range $= \dfrac{Q_{3} - Q_{1}}{2} = \dfrac{46 - 24}{2} = 11$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $22$: 22 is the interquartile range. The semi-interquartile range is half of it.
- $35$: 35 is the average of the quartiles, not half their difference.
- $70$: You added the quartiles.

questions.stem: Find the mean deviation of 1, 5, 6 and 8.
questions.explanation:
Mean $= \dfrac{20}{4} = 5$. Absolute deviations: $4, 0, 1, 3$.

Mean deviation $= \dfrac{4 + 0 + 1 + 3}{4} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $0$: The signed deviations always add up to 0. Mean deviation uses their sizes (absolute values).
- $6.5$: 6.5 is the variance (the mean of the squared deviations).
- $8$: 8 is the total of the absolute deviations. Divide by 4.

papers.title: Ratio, Proportion and Rates: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on ratio, proportion and rates, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Increase Le 450 in the ratio $5 : 3$.
questions.explanation:
New amount $= 450 \times \dfrac{5}{3} = $ Le 750

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Le 1,200: You multiplied by $\dfrac{5 + 3}{3}$. To increase in the ratio 5 : 3, multiply by $\dfrac{5}{3}$.
- Le 1,350: You multiplied by 3 only.
- Le 2,250: You multiplied by 5 only. Divide by 3 as well.

questions.stem: Express a speed of 72 km/h in metres per second.
questions.explanation:
$72$ km/h $= \dfrac{72 \times 1000 \text{ m}}{3600 \text{ s}} = 20$ m/s

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $1.2$ m/s: You divided 72 by 60. There are 3600 seconds in an hour, and 1000 m in a kilometre.
- $259.2$ m/s: You multiplied by 3.6. To change km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6.
- $0.02$ m/s: You divided by 3600 but did not change kilometres to metres (× 1000).

questions.stem: A lorry travels 210 km at an average speed of 60 km/h. How long does the journey take?
questions.explanation:
Time $= \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \dfrac{210}{60} = 3.5$ hours $= 3$ h $30$ min

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3 h 50 min: 3.5 hours is 3 hours and half an hour (30 minutes), not 50 minutes.
- 3 h 5 min: 0.5 of an hour is 30 minutes, not 5 minutes.
- 0 h 17 min: You divided the speed by the distance. Time = distance ÷ speed.

questions.stem: A car uses 8 litres of fuel to travel 100 km. How much fuel does it use to travel 350 km?
questions.explanation:
Fuel per km $= \dfrac{8}{100} = 0.08$ litres. For 350 km: $0.08 \times 350 = 28$ litres.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $2.29$ litres: You divided 8 by 350 and multiplied by 100: the proportion is upside down.
- $3.5$ litres: You worked out $350 \div 100$ and forgot to multiply by 8 litres.
- $43.75$ litres: You divided 350 by 8. The fuel used is $\dfrac{8}{100}$ litres per km.

questions.stem: Abu and Bintu share a profit in the ratio $3 : 5$. Bintu receives Le 1,500 more than Abu. Find the total profit.
questions.explanation:
The difference is $5 - 3 = 2$ parts $= $ Le 1,500, so 1 part $= $ Le 750.

Total $= 8$ parts $= 8 \times 750 = $ Le 6,000

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Le 2,250: Le 2,250 is Abu's share (3 parts).
- Le 3,750: Le 3,750 is Bintu's share (5 parts).
- Le 4,000: You took Le 1,500 as 3 parts. The difference, $5 - 3 = 2$ parts, is Le 1,500.

papers.title: Linear Inequalities: practice set 2
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on linear inequalities, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Solve the inequality $2(x - 3) > 4x + 2$.
questions.explanation:
$2x - 6 > 4x + 2$

$-2x > 8$

Divide by $-2$ and reverse the sign: $x < -4$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $x > -4$: When you divide by $-2$, the inequality sign must be reversed.
- $x < 4$: Check the signs: $-2x > 8$ gives $x < -4$.
- $x > 4$: Both the sign of the answer and the direction of the inequality are wrong.

questions.stem: Find the largest whole number $x$ such that $3x + 7 < 25$.
questions.explanation:
$3x < 18 \Rightarrow x < 6$. The largest whole number less than 6 is 5.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $6$: $x < 6$, so 6 itself is not allowed: $3(6) + 7 = 25$, which is not less than 25.
- $10$: You added 7 instead of subtracting it: $3x < 32$.
- $18$: $3x < 18$, so you must still divide by 3.

questions.stem: Solve $-3 \leq 1 - 2x < 5$.
questions.explanation:
Subtract 1: $-4 \leq -2x < 4$

Divide by $-2$ and reverse the signs: $2 \geq x > -2$, that is $-2 < x \leq 2$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $-2 \leq x < 2$: Dividing by $-2$ reverses both signs, so the strict and non-strict ends swap places.
- $-\dfrac{5}{2} < x \leq \dfrac{3}{2}$: You forgot to subtract 1 from each part first.
- $-4 \leq x < 4$: $-4 \leq -2x < 4$ must still be divided by $-2$.

questions.stem: A taxi charges a fixed Le 10 plus Le 4 for each kilometre. Musa has Le 50. What is the greatest whole number of kilometres he can travel?
questions.explanation:
$10 + 4x \leq 50 \Rightarrow 4x \leq 40 \Rightarrow x \leq 10$

The greatest whole number of kilometres is 10.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $9$: $10 + 4 \times 10 = 50$, which he can afford exactly, so 10 km is allowed.
- $12$: You ignored the fixed charge: $50 \div 4 = 12.5$.
- $15$: You added the fixed charge instead of subtracting it: $60 \div 4$.

questions.stem: On a number line, a solid (filled) dot is drawn at $-1$ with an arrow pointing to the right. Which inequality does this show?
questions.explanation:
A filled dot includes the end value, and an arrow to the right shows larger values: $x \geq -1$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- $x > -1$: A strict inequality is shown by an open (empty) circle, which leaves out $-1$.
- $x \leq -1$: An arrow to the right shows values greater than $-1$.
- $x < -1$: Both the arrow and the dot are misread.
